experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta-v2.md

DeBERTa V2

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of DeBERTaarXiv:2006.03654arXiv:2111.09543arXiv:1910.10683
In one lineDeBERTa with a 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary learned on the training data, relative distances compressed onto log-spaced buckets, position projections shared with the content projections, and a convolution beside the first layer.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

DeBERTa V2 is the architecture the 900M and 1.5B DeBERTa models were trained with, released with the authors' code rather than a paper of its own. It keeps disentangled attention and the enhanced mask decoder and changes four things around them.

  • A larger vocabulary, learned on the training data. 128,000 pieces from SentencePiece replace the 50,000 pieces of GPT-2's byte-level BPE. The embedding table grows to almost half the parameters of the base model.
  • Relative distances are bucketed. Distances up to 128 either way keep a row each. Longer distances share rows spaced on a log scale, up to 255 rows each way, so 512 rows cover what V1 covered with 1,024 and a longer input still finds a row.
  • The position projections are the content projections. The query and key matrices that V1 kept apart for the relative position table are the ones used for content, which removes two matrices per layer.
  • A convolution beside the first layer. A one-dimensional convolution of width three over the input embeddings is added to the output of the first Transformer layer, so that the first layer's output carries the three-token neighbourhood of every token directly. The authors call this n-gram induced input encoding, nGiE.

What the paper adds

There is no V2 paper. The DeBERTa paper's section on the 1.5B model describes the shared projections and the convolution with an ablation on base models showing the sharing costs no accuracy. The repository's release notes add the vocabulary and the buckets. The DeBERTa V3 paper names V2 as the architecture it inherits.

Why it matters here

Two of V2's changes are the ones a Slovenian model would weigh first. The vocabulary is learned on the training text with SentencePiece, which is the Unigram model of this project's tokenizer sweep, so a Slovenian vocabulary drops in without changing the encoder. The bucketed distances are what makes a context past 512 tokens possible for the disentangled design. The convolution is a cheap way to give the first layer the character of a three-token window, which for an inflected language puts a word and its neighbours' endings together.

Facts

Position encodingrelative, bucketed; distances up to 128 keep their own row, longer ones share rows on a log scale, 512 rows in all; absolute position added before the masked-token prediction only
Attention spanevery token attends to every token, as in BERT
Block normalisationpost-norm, as in BERT, with a layer norm on the relative position table
ActivationGELU, as in BERT
Pretraining objectivemasked language modelling on 15% of the tokens, as in RoBERTa
TokenizerSentencePiece, 128,000 pieces learned on the training data
Context length512 tokens in training; the bucketed table reaches any distance
Position buckets256 per side; the scale is stretched so that distance 511 reaches the last bucket
Projectionsthe query and key matrices of the content are applied to the relative position table too
Convolutionkernel 3 over the input embeddings, GELU, added to the first layer's output and normalised; released in the XLarge and XXLarge models
SizesXLarge 24 layers, width 1536, 24 heads, 710M parameters; XXLarge 48 layers, width 1536, 24 heads, 1.32B parameters
Training data160GB, the RoBERTa sources
Optimizeras in DeBERTa

Difference from predecessor

Against DeBERTa: log-bucketed relative distances, shared position projections, a convolution beside the first layer, and a 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary.

DeBERTa2, 3 and the first layer of Algorithm 1 of DeBERTa:the position table has 2k=1024 rows, each distance up to 512 its own row, projected by its own query and key matrices; the first layer is a plain Transformer layer
DeBERTa V22, 3 and the first layer of Algorithm 1 of DeBERTa:512 rows reached through log-spaced buckets, projected by the content's own matrices; a width-three convolution of the input embeddings is added to the first layer's output

Effect. Any distance finds a row at half the table size, two projections per layer disappear, and the first layer sees every token's three-token neighbourhood.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. DeBERTa V2 encoder: convolution beside the first layer and bucketed relative attention

Require: token ids x1,…,xn, embedding table Etok, relative position table P∈ℝ2b×d with b=256 buckets per side, stretch k=512, L layers whose attention follows DeBERTa Algorithm 1 with the changes below

Ensure: hidden states hL

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x])
  2. h1←LN(layer1(h0)+GELU(Conv3(h0)))
  3. for ℓ=2,…,L do
  4. Qr←LN(P)Wq,c, Kr←LN(P)Wk,c, with the content's own matrices of layer ℓ
  5. r←i−j, m←b/2; β(r)←r if |r|≤m, else sign(r)·(⌈log(|r|/m)/log((k−1)/m)·(m−1)⌉+m)
  6. δ(i,j)←β(i−j)+b, clamped to [0,2b−1]
  7. hℓ← DeBERTa Algorithm 1 with these Qr, Kr and δ, then residual, norm and feed-forward as in BERT
  8. return hL

Reading Algorithm 1

1As in DeBERTa, the token embedding enters alone and no position is added at the input.2The first layer runs as in DeBERTa. Beside it a convolution of kernel three slides over the input embeddings, so each output mixes a token with its left and right neighbour. The two results are added and normalised together. The convolution runs on the input only, so layers 2 to L do not have it.3–4In every layer the relative position table is first normalised and then projected by the same query and key matrices the layer uses for content. The two position-only matrices of DeBERTa are gone.5A distance of 128 or less is its own bucket. A longer distance is mapped onto a log scale that reaches bucket 255 at distance 511, so distances from 129 to 511 share 127 buckets, with a bucket covering more distances the further out it lies. The sign is kept, so left and right neighbours never share a row.6The bucket is shifted by b to index the table, and clamped, so a distance beyond 511 reads the outermost row rather than failing.7–8The attention itself is DeBERTa's three-term score with the scale 3d, and everything after it is BERT's layer.

Worked example

The example script ports the bucket rule of the released code to plain Python and applies it to a set of distances, next to the row DeBERTa V1 would read with k=512. The last column counts how many distances from 0 to 511 land in the same row.

Up to distance 128 the two agree except for the offset of the table. From 129 on, V2 starts merging: 150 lands in bucket 143, 200 in 169 with two neighbours, and 400 in 233 with four. V1 keeps every distance up to 511 apart and sends 512, 600 and 1000 to the same outer row. V2 sends them to its outer row too, since the table ends at bucket 255, but a model trained with a stretch k larger than 512 would keep them apart.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The convolution is a release detail

The released base and large V3 models carry no convolution, only the V2 XLarge and XXLarge do. Which sizes it helps is not reported.

Half the parameters of a small model are embeddings

At width 768 the 128,000-piece table holds 98M parameters against 86M in the layers. A small Slovenian model would set the vocabulary size by the tokenizer sweep, not by this release.

Long distances share a row from 129 on

A bucket near 400 covers five distances, so two tokens 398 and 402 apart look the same to the position side. What this costs at a context of 512 is not measured; it is the price of reaching beyond.

the release notes say "log bucket similar to T5". The released code keeps exact distances up to half the bucket count and places the rest with ⌈log(|r|/128)/log(511/128)·127⌉+128, which the worked example computes. T5 uses a fixed number of exact buckets and a different scale.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta-v3.md

DeBERTa V3

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of DeBERTa V2arXiv:2111.09543arXiv:2003.10555
In one lineDeBERTa V2 trained as the discriminator of replaced token detection, with a half-depth generator whose token embeddings it shares while its own gradient is kept from them.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

DeBERTa V3 keeps the V2 encoder and changes what it is trained to do. Instead of predicting masked tokens, the encoder is trained as a discriminator: a smaller generator fills the masked positions with plausible tokens, and the discriminator says, for every position, whether the token there is the original or a replacement. This is the replaced token detection of ELECTRA. The encoder learns from every position rather than from the 15% that were masked.

  • Two models train side by side. The generator is a V2 encoder of the same width and half the depth, trained with masked language modelling. The discriminator is the full V2 encoder with a two-way classifier on every token. Only the discriminator is kept.
  • Token embeddings are shared with a one-way gradient. The discriminator uses the generator's embedding table plus a residual table of its own. The generator's table is updated by the masked-token loss only. The residual table is updated by the detection loss only. After training the two tables are added and saved as the discriminator's.
  • Everything else is V2. Disentangled attention with bucketed distances, shared projections, the 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary, and the 160GB RoBERTa data. The released base and large models carry no convolution.

What the paper adds

The paper's diagnosis is a tug of war. In ELECTRA the two models share one embedding table, and the two losses pull it in opposite directions: masked language modelling draws similar tokens together, detection pushes them apart to make replacements easier to spot. Separate tables train faster but give a worse discriminator, because the generator's embeddings are the better ones. Gradient-disentangled embedding sharing keeps the generator's table as the base and lets the discriminator add only a correction, which the paper shows trains as fast as separate tables and scores higher than either.

Why it matters here

Replaced token detection is the training objective that lets a small encoder make the most of a small corpus, since every token of every sequence yields a training signal. For Slovenian, where the corpus is a hundredth of what the English models saw, that is the lever this entry offers. The objective is independent of the encoder's layers, so it can be paired with any entry of this topic, and an experiment that varies the objective would name this entry.

ActivationGELU, as in BERT

TokenizerSentencePiece, 128,000 pieces, the DeBERTa V2 vocabulary; mDeBERTa uses 250,000 pieces
Context length512 tokens
Generatorsame width as the discriminator, half its depth

Difference from predecessor

Against DeBERTa V2: replaced token detection in place of masked language modelling, with gradient-disentangled embedding sharing.

DeBERTa V2Algorithm 2 of RoBERTa's lineage, the pretraining step, against Algorithm 1 here:one encoder, trained to name the 15% masked tokens
DeBERTa V3Algorithm 2 of RoBERTa's lineage, the pretraining step, against Algorithm 1 here:a half-depth generator names the masked tokens and fills them in; the encoder is trained to tell original tokens from the replacements, at every position, with a shared embedding table whose gradient flows one way

Effect. Every token of every sequence trains the encoder, and the embedding table is shaped by the generator alone with a correction learned by the discriminator.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. One training step of replaced token detection with gradient-disentangled embedding sharing

Require: a sequence x of n tokens, generator G with parameters θG and embedding table EG, discriminator D with parameters θD and residual embedding table EΔ started at zero, weight λ=50

Ensure: updated θG, EG, θD, EΔ

  1. x~G←x with 15% of its positions M masked, replaced as in BERT
  2. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of G(x~G)i against xi
  3. update θG and EG by the gradient of LMLM
  4. x~D←x with each xi, i∈M, replaced by a token sampled from the distribution G(x~G)i, without gradient
  5. ED←sg(EG)+EΔ
  6. LRTD←∑i=1n binary cross-entropy of D(x~D)i against 1[x~D,i≠xi], with D embedding its input through ED
  7. update θD and EΔ by the gradient of λLRTD
  8. return after the last step, save EG+EΔ as the discriminator's embedding table

Reading Algorithm 1

1–2The generator sees BERT's corrupted input and is scored as BERT is, on the masked positions only. It is a V2 encoder of half the depth with the usual prediction head.3The generator and its embedding table learn from the masked-token loss alone. This is the step that, in ELECTRA, also received the detection gradient.4The discriminator's input is the original sequence with the masked positions filled by what the generator proposes. A proposal that happens to equal the original counts as original. Sampling is detached, so no gradient flows from the discriminator into the generator through the tokens.5The discriminator's embedding table is the generator's, read through a stop-gradient so that its own loss cannot change it, plus a residual table of its own. At the first step the residual is zero and the two models embed tokens identically.6Every position is scored, not only the masked ones. The label is whether the token differs from the original. A sequence of 512 tokens gives 512 training signals where masked language modelling gives about 77.7The detection loss, weighted by 50 as in ELECTRA, updates the discriminator's layers and the residual embedding table. The generator's table receives nothing from it, which is what breaks the tug of war.8What is released is the discriminator with one embedding table, the sum of the two, so a downstream user sees an ordinary encoder.

Worked example

The topic's example script holds no V3 example. The training step has no rule to tabulate: its inputs are draws from the generator, and its effect is in the trained weights.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Two encoders in memory during training

The generator adds half an encoder's layers and a second forward pass per step. The paper counts the cost of a step as the same across sharing methods, but it is higher than masked language modelling alone.

The weight 50 is inherited

λ=50 is ELECTRA's value, taken over without a sweep. Whether a smaller model or a smaller corpus wants another weight is not reported.

Masked language modelling is lost as a probe

The released discriminator cannot fill in a blank, so a zero-shot use that asks the model to name a masked word, which a masked language model can do, is not available from this encoder.

A generator the same width as a small model

For a small discriminator the half-depth generator is still a sizeable model, and ELECTRA found that a generator too strong for its discriminator hurts. The paper reports base and larger, not what happens below XSmall.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta.md

DeBERTa

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of RoBERTaarXiv:2006.03654arXiv:1803.02155
In one lineRoBERTa's recipe with attention that scores content and relative position separately, no position at the input, and absolute position added only in the last layers before the masked-token prediction.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

DeBERTa keeps RoBERTa's data, vocabulary and training recipe and changes how the encoder handles position. In BERT and RoBERTa a token's vector is the sum of what it is and where it is, and attention compares those sums. DeBERTa keeps the two apart. Every token has a content vector, and every pair of tokens has a relative position vector that depends only on how far apart they are. Attention adds up three comparisons: content against content, content against the other token's relative position, and this token's relative position against the other's content.

  • Position is not added at the input. The token embedding enters the first layer alone. Distance between tokens is read inside every layer from a shared table of relative position vectors with one row per distance up to 512 either way.
  • Absolute position is added at the end. Where a token stands in the sentence still matters for predicting a masked word, so the model adds the absolute position vectors to the states after the second-to-last layer and runs the last layer twice on that sum. The paper calls this the enhanced mask decoder.
  • Fine-tuning can add scale-invariant perturbation. SiFT, used only for the 1.5B model, normalises the word embeddings before adding the adversarial noise of virtual adversarial training, so the noise is the same size for every token.

What the paper adds

The paper argues that the position-to-content term, which earlier relative position schemes dropped, matters: how much a token attends to a neighbour depends on their distance and on which of the two carries the content. It shows by ablation that removing either position term or the enhanced mask decoder costs accuracy on every benchmark measured. The 1.5B-parameter model was the first to pass the human baseline on SuperGLUE.

Why it matters here

Slovenian word order is freer than English word order, and the case endings carry what the position carries in English. An encoder that reads distance rather than absolute place is a plausible fit for that, and this is the first design in the lineage that does so. The relative position table is also the part a small model can shrink or share across layers without touching the rest. DeBERTa's released vocabulary is RoBERTa's byte-level BPE, so the tokenizer finding carries over.

Difference from predecessor

Against RoBERTa: disentangled attention over content and relative position, with absolute position moved from the input to the decoder.

RoBERTa1 of BERT's Algorithm 1 and line 3 of it, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding, the segment embedding and the absolute position embedding are summed at the input, and attention compares those sums
DeBERTa1 of BERT's Algorithm 1 and line 3 of it, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding enters alone; attention adds a content-to-content, a content-to-position and a position-to-content score read from a shared table of relative distances; absolute position is added before the prediction head

Effect. Every layer reads how far two tokens are apart, and where a token stands is used only to predict the masked word.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Disentangled self-attention in one layer, one head

Require: content states H∈ℝn×d, relative position table P∈ℝ2k×d shared by all layers with k=512, content projections Wq,c,Wk,c,Wv,c, position projections Wq,r,Wk,r

Ensure: attention output Ho∈ℝn×d

  1. Qc←HWq,c, Kc←HWk,c, Vc←HWv,c
  2. Qr←PWq,r, Kr←PWk,r
  3. δ(i,j)←0 if i−j≤−k; 2k−1 if i−j≥k; i−j+k otherwise
  4. A~ij←Qc,iKc,j⊤+Qc,iKr,δ(i,j)⊤+Kc,jQr,δ(j,i)⊤ for every i,j
  5. Ho←softmax(A~/3d)Vc
  6. return Ho

Reading Algorithm 1

1The content side is BERT's attention: a query, a key and a value for every token, from its content vector alone.2The position side projects the shared table once per layer. Row r of Qr and Kr stands for the signed distance r−k, so the table holds every distance from −k to k−1. It is one table for the whole model, and each layer applies its own projections to it.3The signed distance from token i to token j is turned into a row index. Distances beyond k either way share the two outer rows.4Three scores are added. The first asks how well the content of j answers the content of i. The second asks how well the distance to j answers the content of i. The third asks how well the content of j answers the distance from j back to i, which is why its index is δ(j,i). The fourth possible term, position against position, is left out because a distance compared with itself carries nothing.5The sum of three dot products has three times the spread of one, so the scale is 3d rather than BERT's d. The paper reports this factor matters for stable training of large models.6The output has the same shape as BERT's and feeds the same residual, norm and feed-forward steps.

Algorithm 2. Masked language modelling with the enhanced mask decoder

Require: corrupted token ids x with masked positions M, L encoder layers of Algorithm 1, absolute position table Epos, prediction head of BERT

Ensure: the masked-token loss

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x]), with no position embedding
  2. hL−1← layers 1 to L−1 of Algorithm 1 on h0
  3. z←hL−1+Epos[1..n]
  4. for two passes do
  5. z← layer L with query from z and key and value from hL−1
  6. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of the prediction head on zi against the original xi
  7. return LMLM

Reading Algorithm 2

1–2The encoder runs with content only. Through layer L−1 the model knows distances between tokens and nothing about where in the sentence they stand.3The absolute position vectors are added once, to the output of the second-to-last layer. The paper's example is "a new store opened beside the new mall" with both nouns masked: both follow "new" at the same distance, and only the absolute place tells the subject from the object.4–5The last layer is applied twice. The query comes from the position-aware sum, the keys and values from the position-free states, and the second pass reads the first pass's output as its query. The weights of the two passes are the last layer's.6–7The head and the loss are BERT's, on the decoder's output. In fine-tuning the decoder is dropped and the encoder's own last layer is used, so a downstream model never sees absolute position.

Worked example

The topic's example script computes the row index of Algorithm 1, line 3, for a set of distances, next to the bucketed index DeBERTa V2 replaces it with. The table is shown and read in the DeBERTa V2 entry. For V1 every distance from −511 to 511 has its own row and the two outer rows gather everything beyond.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The relative table is fixed at 512 rows

With k=512 the table has 1,024 rows, and an input longer than 512 is not reachable through the position vectors either way, since every distance past 511 reads the same row. DeBERTa V2 compresses long distances onto a log scale instead.

Three scores cost three products

Each layer computes three attention matrices where BERT computes one, and the position side needs two more projections. Inference is slower than RoBERTa's at the same size, and the paper measures accuracy, not speed.

Absolute position reaches only the decoder

A downstream task that depends on where a token stands in the input, rather than on its distance to others, has to recover that from the relative pattern alone, because the fine-tuned encoder never adds the absolute vectors.

Dropping either position term costs accuracy

The paper's ablation shows every benchmark falls when the content-to-position or the position-to-content term is removed, so neither can be dropped to save compute without a loss.

Related

Sources

Paper
DeBERTa: Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention, He, Liu, Gao and Chen, ICLR 2021, arXiv:2006.03654
Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations, Shaw, Uszkoreit and Vaswani, NAACL 2018, arXiv:1803.02155, the relative position scheme DeBERTa extends
Code
none in this repository; the reference implementation is the DebertaModel of the HuggingFace transformers library and the authors' DeBERTa repository
Example
experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/examples.py
Paper vs code
not checked against project code. The paper places the enhanced mask decoder "right after all the Transformer layers"; the authors' released code runs the last encoder layer twice over the states of layer L−1 with the absolute position embeddings added to the query, which is what Algorithm 2 shows.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/modernbert.md

ModernBERT

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of RoBERTaarXiv:2412.13663arXiv:2104.09864arXiv:2002.05202arXiv:2002.04745
In one lineRoBERTa's objective on an encoder rebuilt with rotary position, pre-norm blocks without bias, a gated GELU feed-forward, and attention that alternates every third layer between the whole text and a 128-token window, trained on two trillion tokens to a context of 8,192.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

ModernBERT keeps RoBERTa's training objective, masked language modelling without next-sentence prediction, and rebuilds the encoder with the parts decoder language models settled on between 2019 and 2024. The released base model has 22 layers of width 768 and 149M parameters, the large model 28 layers of width 1024 and 395M. Both read up to 8,192 tokens.

  • Position is rotary. Instead of a learned table, each query and key vector is rotated by an angle that grows with the token's position, so the dot product of two of them depends only on their distance. No position enters the input.
  • Attention alternates. Every third layer, starting with the first, lets every token see the whole text. The other layers let a token see 64 tokens to each side. The global layers use a rotary base of 160,000, the local layers 10,000.
  • The block is pre-norm, without bias. The layer norm sits before the attention and before the feed-forward part, not after the residual addition. Linear layers and norms have no bias term except the final decoder. The feed-forward part is a gated GELU: the input is projected to two halves, one passes through GELU and multiplies the other.
  • Training is long and staged. Two trillion tokens of English web text, code and scientific text, 30% of tokens masked, a batch warmed up to 4,608 sequences, a learning rate held constant for most of the run and decayed at the end. The first 1.7 trillion tokens run at length 1,024, then 250 billion at 8,192, then 50 billion of decay.
  • Padding is removed. Sequences in a batch are concatenated into one stream and attention is told where each begins and ends, so no compute is spent on padding tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that encoders had stood still since RoBERTa while decoders moved, and that porting the decoder changes gives a faster and longer encoder with equal or better scores. The ablations are reported in aggregate; the paper's own comparison is against BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa V3 and the 2024 retrieval encoders on classification, retrieval and code, with a memory and speed table at lengths 512 and 8,192. It also sizes the layers so that every matrix tiles the tensor cores of common GPUs, which it calls hardware-aware design.

Why it matters here

ModernBERT is the current encoder design a small Slovenian model would copy if it copied one. Its parts are separable: rotary position, the local window, the pre-norm block and the gated feed-forward can each be taken or left, and the entry names the line of the algorithm each one sits on. The 8,192-token context matters for document-level extraction, where a relation can span paragraphs. The tokenizer is a byte-level BPE learned on English, so the tokenizer sweep's finding applies, and a Slovenian vocabulary would be the first thing to swap.

Facts

Position encodingrotary, applied to queries and keys in every layer; base 160,000 in global layers, 10,000 in local layers; no position at the input
Attention spanevery third layer, counting from the first, over the whole input; the others over a window of 64 tokens to each side
Block normalisationpre-norm, a layer norm before the attention and before the feed-forward part, without bias; a norm after the embedding and after the last layer; the first layer's attention norm removed
Activationgated GELU, two halves of width 1,152 in base and 2,624 in large
Pretraining objectivemasked language modelling on 30% of the tokens, no next-sentence prediction
Tokenizerbyte-level BPE, 50,368 pieces, a modified OLMo vocabulary with 83 unused slots
Context length8,192 tokens
Biasnone in linear layers or norms, except the decoder of the prediction head
Sizesbase 22 layers, width 768, 12 heads, 149M parameters; large 28 layers, width 1024, 16 heads, 395M parameters
Training data2 trillion tokens of mostly English web text, code and scientific text
OptimizerStableAdamW, AdamW with per-parameter update clipping; learning rate 8e-4 for base held constant after a 3 billion token warmup, 5e-4 for large after 2 billion; decay by 1−t over the last 50 billion tokens
Batch sizewarmed up from 768 to 4,608 sequences over 50 billion tokens for base, 448 to 4,928 over 10 billion for large
Stages1.7 trillion tokens at length 1,024 with rotary base 10,000; 250 billion at length 8,192 at learning rate 3e-4 with the global base raised to 160,000; 50 billion of decay
InitialisationMegatron's for base; large starts from base's weights
Prediction headdense, GELU, layer norm, then a decoder tied to the input embeddings with a bias
Poolingmean of the token vectors for sentence tasks

Difference from predecessor

Against RoBERTa: rotary position, alternating global and local attention, pre-norm blocks without bias, a gated GELU, and a context of 8,192.

RoBERTa1, 3 to 6 and the return of BERT's Algorithm 1, against Algorithm 1 here:token, segment and absolute position embeddings summed at the input; attention over every token; a layer norm after each residual addition; a GELU feed-forward with bias
ModernBERT1, 3 to 6 and the return of BERT's Algorithm 1, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding alone; rotary position applied to queries and keys; attention over the whole text in every third layer and over a 64-token window either side otherwise; a layer norm before each part; a gated GELU without bias

Effect. Distance rather than place reaches every layer, two thirds of the layers cost linear time in the length, and the block trains stably at depth 22 to 28.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. ModernBERT encoder: from token ids to one vector per token

Require: token ids x1,…,xn with n≤8192, embedding table Etok, L layers of width d, window w=64, rotary bases θg=160000 and θl=10000

Ensure: hidden states hL

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x]), with no position or segment embedding and no bias in the norm
  2. for ℓ=1,…,L do
  3. g← true if (ℓ−1)mod3=0, the global layers
  4. u←hℓ−1 if ℓ=1, else LN(hℓ−1)
  5. q,k,v←Wqkvu without bias; rotate qi and ki by the angle of position i with base θg if g else θl
  6. ai←softmaxj(qi·kj/d/A)vj over all j if g, else over j with |i−j|≤w
  7. h←hℓ−1+Woa
  8. (p,z)←WinLN(h) split into two halves; hℓ←h+Wout(GELU(p)⊙z)
  9. return LN(hL)

Reading Algorithm 1

1The input is the token embedding alone, normalised once. Nothing says where a token stands; that enters through the rotation in every layer.2Layers 1, 4, 7 and so on are global, eight of the 22 in base. The rest are local.3Pre-norm: the layer norm is applied to the input of the attention, not to its output. The first layer skips it because the embedding was just normalised.4Queries, keys and values come from one projection without bias. The rotation turns each pair of coordinates of qi and ki by an angle proportional to i, with a frequency per pair set by the base. Because a rotation by i followed by one by −j is a rotation by i−j, the dot product of a rotated query and key depends on their distance only. The larger base of the global layers makes the angles grow more slowly, so distances up to 8,192 stay apart.5A global layer compares every token with every token, at quadratic cost in the length. A local layer compares a token with its 64 neighbours on each side, at linear cost. A token's view widens by 64 to each side per local layer and covers the text at every global one.6The attention output is added to the layer input. No norm follows.7The feed-forward part is gated. One projection produces two halves; GELU of the first half multiplies the second, and a projection narrows the product back. The halves are 1,152 wide in base, so the part has about as many parameters as BERT's feed-forward at inner width 3,072 would at a smaller depth.8A final norm closes the stack, which pre-norm blocks need because no norm follows the last residual addition.

Worked example

The example script lists every layer of the base model with the rule the released code applies: a layer whose index from zero is divisible by three is global, the rest are local with 64 tokens to each side.

Eight of the 22 layers see the whole text, 14 see a window of 129 tokens. At length 8,192 a local layer compares each token with 129 others where a global layer compares it with 8,192, so the local layers are about one sixtieth of the attention cost at full length.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The vocabulary is English

The 50,368-piece byte-level BPE was learned on English and code. Slovenian text is spelled in more tokens per word than with a vocabulary learned on Slovenian, which lengthens every input and spends the context on pieces.

The recipe assumes two trillion tokens

The staged schedule, the batch warmup and the constant learning rate are tuned to a run that no Slovenian corpus can fill. What the design gives at a hundredth of the data is not in the paper.

Ablations are not broken out

The paper reports the parts together and names the earlier work each came from. Which of the five changes carries the gain over RoBERTa is not separated, which is the question an experiment here would ask.

Local layers see 129 tokens

A dependency longer than 64 tokens is carried only by the eight global layers, or by stacking local layers. The paper measures retrieval and classification, not a task where one long-range link decides the answer.

Speed needs the unpadded kernels

The memory and speed figures rely on Flash Attention with variable-length sequences. Without those kernels the alternating pattern still saves compute in principle but not the measured factor.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/roberta.md

RoBERTa

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of BERTarXiv:1907.11692
In one lineBERT's encoder unchanged, retrained with a fresh mask on every pass, full sentences packed across document boundaries, no next-sentence prediction, a byte-level BPE vocabulary, and ten times the data at a batch of 8,000 sequences.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

RoBERTa is BERT trained differently. The layers, the widths, the absolute position table and the masking rule are all BERT's. What changes is how the training examples are made and how long and how large the training runs. The paper's point is that these choices, which BERT left under-explored, are worth as much as a new architecture.

  • The mask is drawn anew every time a sequence is seen. BERT fixed the mask when the corpus was prepared. RoBERTa draws it when the sequence is fed to the model, so every pass over the data hides different tokens.
  • Inputs are full sentences packed to 512 tokens. Sentences are taken in order from the stream of documents until the input is full. When a document ends, a separator is added and the next document continues in the same input. There is no second segment and no next-sentence label.
  • Text is cut by byte-level BPE. The vocabulary of 50,000 pieces is GPT-2's, learned over bytes, so no character is ever unknown.
  • Training is longer and wider. 160GB of text instead of 16GB, batches of 8,000 sequences instead of 256, 500,000 steps, and every step at the full length of 512 tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper is a controlled study of BERT's training recipe. It reruns BERT with one change at a time and shows which of them move the benchmarks: dynamic masking slightly, dropping next-sentence prediction slightly, larger batches and more data and longer training considerably. The byte-level vocabulary costs a little on some tasks but removes unknown tokens, which the authors take as worth it. The resulting recipe became the default for most encoders that followed.

Why it matters here

The Slovenian encoder most often used as a baseline, SloBERTa, is a RoBERTa trained with the CamemBERT recipe, so RoBERTa is the closest published design to what a Slovenian-only encoder has looked like. Its lesson for a small model is that data, batch size and training length are the first dials to set, before any change to the layers. Its byte-level vocabulary is also the byte-level BPE of this project's tokenizer sweep, so the sweep's finding on Slovenian morphology applies to this design directly.

Facts

Position encodinglearned absolute, as in BERT
Attention spanevery token attends to every token, as in BERT
Block normalisationpost-norm, as in BERT
ActivationGELU, as in BERT
Pretraining objectivemasked language modelling on 15% of the tokens with a fresh mask on every pass; no next-sentence prediction
Tokenizerbyte-level BPE, 50,000 pieces, the GPT-2 vocabulary
Context length512 tokens, every training step at full length
Inputfull sentences taken in order across document boundaries up to 512 tokens, a separator between documents, one segment for all tokens
SizesBase and Large as in BERT, 125M and 355M parameters with the larger vocabulary
Training dataBookCorpus and Wikipedia 16GB, CC-News 76GB, OpenWebText 38GB, Stories 31GB, in all over 160GB
OptimizerAdam with β2=0.98 and ϵ=10−6 for stability at the large batch, peak learning rate 6e-4 for Base and 4e-4 for Large, warmup over 30,000 and 24,000 steps, linear decay, weight decay 0.01
Training length500,000 steps of 8,000 sequences of 512 tokens, about two trillion tokens seen

Difference from predecessor

Against BERT: dynamic masking, full-sentence packing, no next-sentence prediction, a byte-level BPE vocabulary, and ten times the data at a batch of 8,000.

BERT1 to 3 and the return of Algorithm 1, against lines 1 to 3 and 9 of BERT's Algorithm 2:two segments, half of them unrelated, a mask drawn once when the corpus is prepared, and the sum of the masked-token and next-sentence losses
RoBERTa1 to 3 and the return of Algorithm 1, against lines 1 to 3 and 9 of BERT's Algorithm 2:full sentences packed across documents, a mask drawn each time the sequence is fed, and the masked-token loss alone

Effect. Every pass over the data shows a different masking, every input is 512 tokens of real text, and the encoder itself is untouched.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. RoBERTa pretraining example: dynamic masking over packed full sentences

Require: a stream of documents, byte-level BPE vocabulary V of 50,000 pieces, maximum length T=512

Ensure: one input sequence and its masked-token targets

  1. take full sentences in order from the stream until T tokens are reached; when a document ends, add a separator token and continue with the next document
  2. x← <s> sentences </s>, with one segment id for every token
  3. M← 15% of the token positions of x, drawn at random now, each time x is fed to the model
  4. for all i∈M do
  5. with probability 0.8 replace xi by <mask>; with 0.1 by a random token of V; with 0.1 keep xi
  6. h← the BERT encoder (BERT, Algorithm 1) on x
  7. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of the prediction head against the original xi
  8. return LMLM

Reading Algorithm 1

1An input is filled with consecutive sentences until the length is reached, so almost every input is 512 tokens of text that belongs together. A document boundary inside the input is marked by a separator and not avoided. The paper also tried stopping at the document boundary, which scored slightly higher but gave batches of uneven size, and kept the packed form for the fixed batch size.2There is one segment, so the segment embedding carries no information. The special tokens are the start and end markers of the byte-level vocabulary.3–5The mask is drawn at the moment the sequence enters the model. Across the 500,000 steps the same sentence is hidden in a different place each time it is seen. The replacement rule inside the mask is BERT's.6–7The encoder and the prediction head are BERT's. Only the masked positions are scored.8There is no second loss. The paper found that removing next-sentence prediction matched or improved every task it measured.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The encoder is BERT's

Position is still absolute and told once, attention still spans every token, and the context is still 512. The paper changes nothing a later entry would call architecture.

A byte-level vocabulary spends pieces on bytes

The 256 byte symbols and the merges built from them are learned on English web text. A character of a language that is not English costs several bytes before it becomes a piece of its own, so a vocabulary learned on English spells Slovenian text in more tokens than a vocabulary learned on Slovenian.

The recipe is expensive

A batch of 8,000 sequences of 512 tokens for 500,000 steps is about two trillion tokens seen, over 1,000 GPUs. A small model trained on a small corpus repeats the data many times instead, and the paper does not say what happens then.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/README.md

Information Extraction

open4 entries0 checked

Which zero-shot extraction head should a small Slovenian encoder carry, and which of its parts decide what the model can return and what it can never return?

Zero-shot information extraction asks a model for entity types, labels or relations it was never trained on, named at the moment of the request. The entries here are one lineage of encoder-based extractors. Each one writes the request into the input as a prompt, runs a bidirectional encoder once over prompt and text, and matches the vectors of the request against the vectors of the text. What changes from one generation to the next is the prompt grammar, which text units are scored, how many of them, and what the decoder is allowed to return. The Compared table puts those parts side by side so an experiment can name the one it varies.

GLiNER

from paperin topic Information ExtractionarXiv:2311.08526arXiv:2111.09543
In one lineEntity type names and the text go through one bidirectional encoder, every span of up to 12 words is scored against every type name by a sigmoid dot product, and the spans above 0.5 are kept greedily without overlap.
DescriptionAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

GLiNER, a generalist model for named entity recognition, finds entities of types it was never trained on. The user writes the type names, such as "person" or "organisation", and the model prepends them to the text. One bidirectional encoder reads prompt and text together, so the vector of each type name has seen the text and the vector of each word has seen the type names. The model then treats recognition as matching: every span of at most 12 words gets one vector, every type name gets one vector, and the sigmoid of their dot product says whether the span is an entity of that type. All spans and all types are scored in one pass, which is what makes it faster than a generative model that writes entities out one token at a time.

  • The prompt is part of the input. A marker token stands before each type name and a separator token closes the prompt. Both markers are new tokens whose embeddings are learned during training.
  • A span is its two ends. The span vector is built from the vector of its first word and the vector of its last word, each passed through a small feed-forward layer, then joined and projected back to the encoder width.
  • Scoring is a dot product. No head knows the type names in advance; a type is whatever its name's vector says, which is what lets the model take new types at inference.
  • Decoding is greedy. Candidates above the threshold are sorted by score and taken in order, each one skipped if it overlaps a span already taken.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that a 300M-parameter encoder, trained once on a corpus of 13k entity types produced by prompting a large language model, beats ChatGPT and fine-tuned generative models on zero-shot entity recognition at a fraction of the cost. It trains on Pile-NER, 44,889 passages annotated by GPT-3.5 with 240k spans, and evaluates on 20 benchmarks the model never saw, in English and in seven other languages through the multilingual DeBERTa backbone. Two regularisations matter for the claim: entity types are shuffled and some are dropped at random so the model cannot learn their order, and negative types drawn from other examples teach it to return nothing for a type the text does not contain.

Why it matters here

GLiNER is the extraction head a small Slovenian encoder would carry first, because its output is exactly what this project's task data holds. The span converter in slm4ie/data/tasks/converters/spans.py:1-14 writes every Slovenian NER dataset as GLiNER-style rows, text plus start, end and label per span, so a GLiNER head can be fine-tuned and evaluated on them without another conversion. The head is also separable from the backbone: the released multilingual model sits on mDeBERTa-v3-base, and the encoders of the encoder-transformers topic are the candidates to put under it.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER inference: type names and text through one encoder, every span scored against every type

Require: words w1,…,wN, type names t1,…,tM, encoder E, span width K=12, threshold τ=0.5

Ensure: a set R of typed, non-overlapping spans (i,j,m)

  1. x←[ENT]t1…[ENT]tM[SEP]w1…wN
  2. H←E(x); pm← the vector at the m-th [ENT]; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  3. qm←FFNt(pm) for every type m
  4. for all (i,j) with 1≤i≤j≤min(i+K−1,N) do
  5. sij←FFNo(ReLU(FFNs(hi)⊕FFNe(hj)))
  6. ϕ(i,j,m)←σ(sij·qm) for every type m
  7. C←{(i,j,m):ϕ(i,j,m)>τ}, sorted by ϕ descending
  8. R←∅
  9. for all (i,j,m)∈C do
  10. if no span in R overlaps [i,j] then
  11. R←R∪{(i,j,m)}
  12. return R

Reading Algorithm 1

1The prompt is text. Each type name follows its own marker, and the separator keeps the encoder from reading the last type name into the first word. Nothing about the types is stored in the model.2One encoder pass gives every token a vector that has seen prompt and text. The type vector is read at the marker, not at the name, so a type of several words still gives one vector. A word of several subwords is read at its first subword.3A two-layer feed-forward network turns the marker vector into the type vector. The same network serves every type.4Candidate spans are every start with every width up to K, so a text of N words has about NK of them. The limit keeps the count linear in the length and discards nothing the benchmarks contain, where entities rarely exceed 12 words.5The span vector comes from its two ends. Each end is projected on its own, the two are joined, and one more projection brings the pair back to the encoder width. A span of one word uses the same vector twice.6The score is a dot product squashed to a probability. Every span and type pair is scored at once as one matrix product, which is where the parallel extraction comes from.7Only pairs above the threshold are candidates. Sorting by score decides which of two overlapping candidates wins.8** to **12Greedy decoding. A candidate is kept unless it overlaps a kept span; in the nested mode a span fully inside a kept span is also allowed. The set returned is the set of entities.

Algorithm 2. GLiNER training: one batch

Require: examples (w,G) with gold spans G⊆{(i,j,m)}, the types of the other examples in the batch, limits of 25 types per example

Ensure: updated encoder and projection weights

  1. for each example, take its gold types, add negative types drawn from the batch at a ratio of at most 1 to 1, shuffle, drop some at random, and cut to 25
  2. compute ϕ(i,j,m) for every span and type pair as Algorithm 1, lines 1 to 6
  3. y(i,j,m)←1 if (i,j,m)∈G else 0
  4. L←−∑(i,j,m)[ylogϕ+(1−y)log(1−ϕ)]
  5. return one AdamW step on L, at 10−5 for the encoder and 5·10−5 for the projections

Reading Algorithm 2

1The type list is rebuilt for every example. Negative types teach the model to return nothing for a type the text lacks. Shuffling and dropping keep it from learning a type's position.2Training scores the same span grid inference does, so there is no train-and-test gap in what is scored.3** and **4Every span and type pair is a binary decision. Gold spans are positives; all other pairs, including gold spans under the wrong type, are negatives.5The encoder moves slowly and the fresh projections faster. The paper runs 30,000 such steps with a cosine schedule.

Worked example

The example script lays out the prompt the released multilingual model builds for one Slovenian sentence with two type names, and counts the spans it scores at several text lengths.

A text of 32 words gives 318 spans per type. At 512 words the grid is 6,078 spans per type, still linear in the length because the width is capped, but each span is scored against every type, so a prompt of 20 types at 512 words scores over 120,000 pairs.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Twelve words is a hard ceiling

A span of 13 or more words cannot be returned, whatever the score. Titles of works, addresses and legal citations in Slovenian text exceed it.

The prompt eats the context

Type names and the text share 384 subword tokens. Twenty Slovenian type names spelled by an English-trained tokenizer take a large share of it before the text begins.

Spans only

One span, one type. A relation between two spans, a label for the whole text, or an attribute of a span has no place in the output.

Silver training data

Pile-NER was annotated by GPT-3.5 with no human check, and its types are whatever the annotator named. What the model learned as "person" is that annotator's notion of a person.

Paper vs code
not checked against project code. Three differences against the released package. The paper names the markers [ENT] and [SEP]; the code uses <<ENT>> and <<SEP>>. The paper builds a span vector by one feed-forward layer over the joined end vectors; the default span mode projects each end separately, joins them, applies ReLU and projects once more. The paper trains with binary cross-entropy; the code's default is focal loss, which reduces to binary cross-entropy at its default settings, with half of the negative span and type pairs dropped from the loss at random.

GLiNER2.5

from paperin topic Information Extractionvariant of GLiNER2arXiv:2507.18546
In one lineGLiNER2's schema prompt on a boundary head that scores where spans start and end instead of enumerating a span grid, pairs the best boundaries sparsely so a span may have any length, adds typed relations and span attributes, and hands every score to a constrained decoder on a 4,096-word context.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

GLiNER2.5 keeps GLiNER2's prompt and encoder and replaces the span grid. For each request, called a query, the model scores every token boundary as a possible start, every token boundary as a possible end, and every token as being inside a span of that query. A proposal stage keeps the best starts and, for each, the best ends that follow it, then the same backwards from the best ends, and the union, cut to a budget, is the candidate set. Each candidate pair is then rescored with the inside evidence between its ends and its length. Because a start may pair with any later end, a span can open at the first token and close at the last, and the work stays linear in the text length for a fixed schema and budget.

  • Relations are typed pairs of mentions. A relation group names a head role and a tail role, and the schema says which entity types may fill each. For every relation type the best head-typed and tail-typed mentions are paired and scored together with the relation's query vector.
  • Attributes classify a span. An attribute such as sentiment or negation is a classification whose query is scored on an already extracted span, so a mention carries its own labels.
  • Records lose the count head. A record is formed around an anchor field; every anchor candidate seeds one record and the other fields are assigned to a record or declared absent.
  • Decoding is constrained. Classification tasks may declare rules between labels, relations declare their endpoint types and multiplicity, and the decoder returns only assignments that satisfy them; the type-safe-encoder entry describes it.

What the paper adds

There is no paper. The release note states three claims: a span may have any length within the window, inference stays linear in the length, and outputs satisfy the declared schema. On the vendor's zero-shot suite the multilingual model scores level with GLiNER2 overall and far above it on natural language inference, and its training data was generated by the vendor's own data agent rather than drawn from public corpora.

Why it matters here

GLiNER2.5 is the current shape of the head this project would train, and the first whose candidate count does not grow with a width limit: a Slovenian document of 4,000 words is scored on 192 candidates per query instead of a grid of tens of thousands. Its relation and attribute heads cover what the NER benchmarks here do not. The cost is that none of its parts has a paper and the recipe exists only as code, so what a Slovenian backbone would need of it is read from the implementation.

Facts

Tasksnamed entity recognition, classification, record extraction, typed relation extraction, span attributes, and any combination in one pass
Prompt tokensGLiNER2's, plus [R] before the head and tail roles of a relation group
Span candidatesfor each query, the top k starts by start score paired with the 12 best ends after each, the same from the top k ends backwards, duplicates removed, cut to 192; k is 24, raised with the length to at most 128
Longest spanthe text; no width limit
Scoringstart, end and inside scores as scaled dot products between the query vector and boundary or token vectors; a candidate's logit is the pair's endpoint compatibility plus its start and end scores plus the mean inside score between them plus length and content terms
Decodingcandidates with sigmoid above 0.5, or filled up to a predicted count, under a flat overlap policy; relations over the 32 best head and tail mentions per type, at most 64 pairs; classification and relations then pass through the constrained decoder
BackboneDeBERTa-v3-base for the base model, mDeBERTa-v3-base for the multilingual one, a 74M small model
Context length4,096 words
Training datagenerated by the vendor's data agent; size not published
Boundary headboundary vectors of width 128 from the left and right token vectors, two local attention blocks with a window of 128 and one gated feed-forward block; the pair scorer has width 128 with 8 compatibility heads and rotary endpoint positions
Trainingan asymmetric focal loss over start and end scores, binary cross-entropy over candidate pairs with 20 hard negatives per positive, a listwise loss that ranks gold pairs first, a Poisson loss on the count head, binary cross-entropy on labels and relations, weighted and summed
Sizessmall 74M, base 0.2B, multilingual 0.3B parameters

Difference from predecessor

Against GLiNER2: a sparse boundary proposal replaces the width-limited span grid; relations, attributes and constrained decoding are added.

GLiNER24 of GLiNER2's Algorithm 1, the span grid, against lines 2 to 8 of Algorithm 1 here:every span of at most 8 words is built from its two end vectors and scored against each field vector
GLiNER2.54 of GLiNER2's Algorithm 1, the span grid, against lines 2 to 8 of Algorithm 1 here:boundary vectors are scored as starts and ends per query, the best are paired sparsely at any distance, and each pair is rescored with the inside evidence between its ends

Effect. A span may be as long as the text, the candidate count is a fixed budget rather than length times width, and relations and label rules enter the output.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER2.5 inference: boundary scores, sparse pairing and rescoring, one query

Require: words w1,…,wN, a schema prompt as GLiNER2 with [R] roles, encoder E, budgets k0=24, α=0.08, kmax=128, ends per start e=12, candidate budget C=192, threshold τ=0.5

Ensure: scored spans per query, handed to the constrained decoder

  1. H←E(x) with x as GLiNER2's Algorithm 1, line 1; u← the vector at the query's field marker; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  2. bi←LN(Wo[Wlhi⊕Wrhi+1]) for the N+1 boundaries, with learned vectors before w1 and after wN; two attention blocks over a window of 128 boundaries and one gated feed-forward block refine b
  3. ai←⟨Wsbi,Ws′u⟩/d, ei←⟨Webi,We′u⟩/d, ni←⟨Wnhi,Wn′u⟩/d: start, end and inside scores
  4. k←min(kmax,⌈max(k0,⌈αN⌉)/8⌉·8); S← the k boundaries with the largest ai; T← the k with the largest ei
  5. P←{(i,j):i∈S,j among the e ends after i with the largest ⟨g(u)⊙Wpbi,Wqbj⟩+ej}∪{(i,j):j∈T,i among the e starts before j likewise}
  6. Cq← the C pairs of P with the largest proposal score, duplicates removed
  7. for all (i,j)∈Cq do
  8. ℓij←compat(bi,bj,u)+ai+ej+priorij+ω(u)·∑i≤t<jnt/j−i+λ(u)·len(i,j)+content(i,j,u)
  9. Rq←{(i,j):σ(ℓij)≥τ}, extended to the count head's predicted number when adaptive, overlaps resolved by score
  10. relations: for each relation type, the 32 best head-typed and 32 best tail-typed mentions of R, at most 64 pairs, scored by a bilinear layer over the two mention vectors and the relation's query
  11. labels: σ(MLPl(ug,k)) per label marker; attributes: the attribute query scored on each extracted span of the types it applies to
  12. return every candidate with its score, for the constrained decoder

Reading Algorithm 1

1The prompt and encoder are GLiNER2's. Each field marker, including the head and tail roles of a relation, is one query with its own vector.2A boundary sits between two words. Its vector joins the word on its left and the word on its right, so the start of a span is described by what precedes it and what it begins with. Learned vectors stand in for the missing neighbour at the two ends of the text. Local attention lets boundaries see 128 neighbours and a feed-forward block refines them.3Three scores per query, each a scaled dot product with the query vector: how much a boundary looks like a start, how much like an end, and how much a token looks like part of the span. The inside scores are summed into a running total so any interval's inside evidence is one subtraction.4The budget grows with the length, from 24 boundaries to at most 128, rounded up to a multiple of 8 so batches share shapes. The top starts and the top ends are chosen by their scores alone.5Each chosen start is paired with the 12 ends after it that fit it best, by a gated dot product between the two boundary vectors plus the end score; each chosen end is paired with the 12 starts before it likewise. No term depends on the distance, which is what removes the width limit. At most 2·k·e pairs are ever materialised.6The two directions are merged, duplicates collapsed, and the 192 best pairs kept. This is the candidate set; nothing outside it can be returned.7** and **8Each candidate is rescored with everything known about it: the endpoint compatibility through 8 heads, its start and end scores, the proposal score as a prior, the mean inside score of the tokens between its ends, three length features, and a pooled vector of its content. The query decides how much the inside and length terms weigh.9A candidate is an entity if its sigmoid clears the threshold. With adaptive decoding, a count head's Poisson rate fills the list up to the predicted number. The flat policy drops a candidate that overlaps a better one.10Relations reuse the extracted mentions. The schema says which types may be a head and which a tail, so only typed pairs are formed, and a cap keeps the pair count fixed. A bilinear scorer reads both mention vectors and the relation's query.11Labels are classified from their markers as in GLiNER2. An attribute is a classification run on a span: the attribute's query is scored on each extracted span of the types it applies to.12Nothing is final here. Candidates, relations and labels go to the constrained decoder, which decides what the schema allows.

Worked example

The candidate-counts table compares the span grids of the two predecessors with the boundary budget at several lengths, computed with the released configuration's rule.

Up to 128 words the budget stays at 24 starts and 24 ends; at 512 it is 48 and from about 1,600 words it is capped at 128. The pairs proposed grow from 576 to 3,072, and the candidates actually rescored never exceed 192 per query, where GLiNER2's grid at 4,096 words holds 32,740 spans per type.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

No paper

The method, its losses and its training data are described in a release note and a model card. The claims are the vendor's own benchmarks. An experiment here would be the first independent measurement.

A span outside the budget is lost

If a gold span's start is not among the k best starts, or its end not among the 12 best ends for that start or the reverse, it is never scored. Recall on long or unusual spans depends on the proposer, and the proposer is trained with gold pairs injected, which inference lacks.

The budget is per query, the pool per text

The shared candidate pool is built once from the start and end scores of all queries, so a query with few strong boundaries competes with the others for the same 192 slots.

Thresholds and budgets are tuned to the vendor's data

Every number above, from the window of 128 to the 20 hard negatives, is a configuration value chosen on undisclosed training data. Which of them a Slovenian retraining must keep is unknown.

not checked against project code. The release note says the model predicts start and end scores and pairs them without a width limit; the code also scores every token as inside, keeps a running sum of those scores so any interval's inside evidence costs one subtraction, and adds length features and a pooled content vector to each candidate. The note says 4,096 words; the configuration's limit is 4,096 and the boundary attention sees a window of 128 boundaries. experiments/reference/information-extraction/gliner2.md

GLiNER2

from paperin topic Information Extractionvariant of GLiNERarXiv:2507.18546
In one lineGLiNER's span matching behind a schema prompt that composes entity types, classification labels and record fields in one input, with a count head for how many records to fill and a label head for classification, on a 2,048-token context.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedSourcesjk sections

Description

GLiNER2 keeps GLiNER's idea, one encoder over prompt and text and a dot product between request vectors and span vectors, and widens what a request may be. The request is a schema: a list of entity types, a classification task with its labels, or a record type with named fields, and several of these at once. Each part of the schema becomes a bracketed group in the prompt with its own marker tokens, the groups are joined by a separator, and the text follows. One forward pass then serves every group.

  • Entities work as in GLiNER. Each type marker's vector is matched against every span of at most 8 words.
  • Records are entities with a count. A record type such as "employment" has fields such as "employee" and "employer". A small head reads the group's prompt marker and predicts how many records the text holds, from 0 to 19. For each record, a recurrent layer stamps the field vectors with the record's index, and each stamped field vector is matched against the spans as an entity type would be. The result is a list of filled records rather than a flat list of spans.
  • Classification reads the label markers. Each label's marker vector goes through a small classifier that outputs one logit. A single-label task takes the largest; a multi-label task keeps every label above 0.5.
  • Descriptions and examples ride in the prompt. A type or label may carry a short description and a task may carry a few labelled examples, written after the group's name behind their own marker tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that one encoder under 500M parameters can replace a large language model for entity recognition, text classification and structured extraction at once, on a CPU. It trains a 205M-parameter model on 254,334 examples, 135,698 from news, Wikipedia, legal text, arXiv and PubMed annotated by GPT-4o and 118,636 synthetic ones from emails, messages, resumes and e-commerce text, and reports results against GLiNER and against prompted large models on zero-shot NER, classification and record extraction. The released package adds a schema builder and LoRA fine-tuning.

Why it matters here

GLiNER2 is the first entry whose output covers more than entity spans, which is what a Slovenian extraction benchmark beyond NER would need: sentiment and the SuperGLUE-SL tasks this project prepares are classification, and a record schema fits event-like annotations. Its parts are separable from the backbone in the same way GLiNER's are, so a Slovenian encoder can take the span head, the count head and the label head as they stand. The multilingual release again sits on mDeBERTa-v3-base.

Facts

GLiNER1 and 4 to 11 of Algorithm 1 against GLiNER's Algorithm 1:one prompt of type names, every span of at most 12 words scored against every type, greedy decoding

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER2 inference: one forward pass over a composed schema

Require: words w1,…,wN, schema groups g1,…,gG each with a name and fields fg,1,…,fg,k, encoder E, span width K=8

Ensure: entities per type, filled records per record type, labels per classification task

  1. x←group(g1)[SEP_STRUCT]…group(gG)[SEP_TEXT]w1…wN, with group(g)=([P] name (μ fg,1…μ fg,k)) and μ one of [E], [C], [L]
  2. H←E(x); pg← the vector at the [P] of group g; ug,k← the vector at its k-th field marker; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  3. for all entity groups g do
  4. score every span (i,j) with j−i<K against every ug,k as GLiNER's Algorithm 1, lines 4 to 12
  5. for all record groups g do
  6. n←\argmaxc∈0..19MLPc(pg)
  7. ug,k(r)←T(GRU(er,ug,k)+ug,k) for r=1..n, with er a learned embedding of the record index and T a small transformer
  8. record r, field k← the span with the highest σ(sij·ug,k(r)), or every span above 0.5 for a list field
  9. for all classification groups g do
  10. zg,k←MLPl(ug,k); single-label: the k with the largest z; multi-label: every k with σ(zg,k)>0.5
  11. return the entities, records and labels

Reading Algorithm 1

1Every request becomes a bracketed group. The group's name follows the prompt marker, its fields follow their own marker, and the marker's kind says what the fields are: entity types, record fields or labels. Several groups sit in one prompt, which is what lets one pass serve several tasks.2As in GLiNER, vectors are read at the markers. Each group gives one prompt vector and one vector per field.3** and **4Entity groups are plain GLiNER with a shorter width. Every span of at most 8 words is scored against every type vector and decoded greedily.5** and **6A record group first decides how many records the text holds. The classifier over the prompt vector has 20 outputs, 0 to 19, and the largest wins.7Each record needs its own field vectors, or every record would fill the same spans. A learned embedding of the record index is fed with the field vector through a GRU, the field vector is added back, and a two-layer transformer lets the fields of one record see each other.8A stamped field vector is matched against the spans exactly as a type vector is. The best span fills the field; a field declared as a list takes every span above threshold.9** and **10Classification never looks at spans. Each label's marker vector goes through a classifier that outputs one logit. A single-label task takes the largest logit; a multi-label task thresholds each one.11One structured answer: lists of spans per type, lists of records per record type, labels per task.

Worked example

The prompt-layouts table shows the input the released processor builds for the toy sentence with an entity group, a classification group, a record group and all of them composed, and the candidate-counts table shows how many spans the width of 8 yields.

The shorter width cuts the grid by about a third against GLiNER at every length, from 318 to 228 spans per type at 32 words.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Eight words is a harder ceiling than twelve

A span of nine or more words cannot be returned. Slovenian organisation names and titles exceed it more often than English ones.

Nineteen records at most

The count head has 20 outputs. A text with more records than that fills nineteen and drops the rest.

No relations

Two spans can share a record but the model never scores a pair of spans as such. A relation type with head and tail roles arrives only in GLiNER2.5.

Tasks do not see each other's answers

Each group is decoded on its own. A label combination the schema forbids, such as a harm type under a "safe" verdict, can be returned, which is what the type-safe decoding of the successor exists to prevent.
